pll1d32c4-d1e3501.summary: Reports the argument that the Father has more than one wisdom: the Son is the Father's begotten wisdom by which he is not wise, and unbegotten wisdom is that by which he is wise; so there are two.

pll1d32c4-d1e3504.summary: Adds another argument: unbegotten and begotten wisdom are each the Father's wisdom, but not the same; so the Father does not have only one wisdom.

pll1d32c4-d1e3507.summary: Rejects such arguments as sophistical and unworthy of answer, adding that there is one wisdom of the Father said in different ways: the begotten is his because he begot it, the unbegotten because he is wise by it. Yet they are one wisdom, since the persons signified by begotten and unbegotten wisdom are the one wisdom, the essence common to three.
claims: There is one wisdom of the Father under different reasons of predication.

pl-l1d32c4.summary: Rejects as sophistical the arguments that the Father has more than one wisdom (begotten wisdom by which he is not wise, and unbegotten wisdom by which he is). There is one wisdom of the Father, said in different ways: the Son is the Father's wisdom because he begot it; the unbegotten is his because he is wise by it. Yet begotten wisdom is the same wisdom, since the persons of Father and Son, signified as unbegotten and begotten wisdom, are the one wisdom that is the divine essence common to all three.
claims: Arguments that the Father has two wisdoms are sophistical.
There is one wisdom of the Father, said in different senses.
The Son is the Father's wisdom because the Father begot it.
Unbegotten wisdom is the Father's because he is wise by it.
Begotten and unbegotten wisdom are one wisdom, the common divine essence.
